sections.overview: Alpacas are Andean domestic camelids, raised in herds chiefly for their fleece. Genetic studies identify the vicuña as their main wild ancestor; domestic herds also show later llama ancestry. Also known historically as Vicugna pacos, the species is currently listed as Lama pacos by the Mammal Diversity Database.
sections.identification: Adults usually stand about 0.8–1.0 metres at the shoulder and weigh roughly 45–90 kilograms, with size varying by sex, condition and population. Alpacas are smaller and more lightly built than llamas. Huacaya fleece is dense and crimped; Suri fibre grows in long, silky locks. Each foot has two small-nailed toes supported by broad pads, while the split upper lip and lower incisors help crop short plants.
sections.habitat: Domestic herds are centred in the high Andes of Peru and Bolivia, with husbandry also extending into northern Chile. Alpacas graze open puna grasslands, dry slopes and wet valley meadows called bofedales, moving as forage and water change. In one Bolivian pastoral system, herders relied more heavily on wet meadows during the dry season.
sections.diet: They crop short plants with a split upper lip and lower incisors, then chew repeatedly. Anatomical examination found that the alpaca stomach has three compartments, rather than the four in true ruminants. Microbial fermentation occurs chiefly in the first compartment, where fibrous forage is broken down before further digestion. This digestive design helps alpacas use coarse plants, while forage quality and abundance still change with season. Herders may add hay when grazing is scarce.
sections.behavior: Alpacas live in social herds. They communicate through posture, ear position, vocal sounds and spitting or retreating during conflict. A soft hum can accompany contact or routine activity, but also separation or distress; it does not always signal calm. A sharper alarm call can alert nearby animals to perceived danger.
sections.reproduction: Females do not follow a regular spontaneous oestrous cycle: mating stimulates ovulation, a pattern called induced ovulation. Gestation lasts about eleven months and usually produces one cria, the term for a young camelid. A cria is relatively developed at birth and soon stands to follow its mother. Mothers nurse and protect their young, which are commonly weaned near six months.
sections.ecology: Bofedales are wet meadows within the seasonally dry puna; their water and low-growing plants provide important forage for alpacas and other livestock. A study of natural and irrigated bofedales in southern Peru found links among vegetation, soil and hydrology, with similar carbon storage and palatable plant cover in the two sites. The researchers found that cover of two nutritious alpaca forage plants tracked environmental measurements weakly, suggesting grazing may obscure those relationships.
sections.conservation: The Mammal Diversity Database classifies the alpaca as domesticated and marks it Not Evaluated on the global Red List. A genomic study dated substantial llama-to-alpaca introgression to about 500 years ago, near the Spanish conquest; the authors suggest disrupted traditional management may explain the pattern but say its cause is unknown. In a 1995–96 Bolivian study, deferred grazing (temporarily resting pasture) reduced plant diversity in bofedales but access to reserves improved young alpaca survival. The authors caution that fencing communal pastures can bring social costs.
